# Accounts hub

## Use when

Use this pattern when one person or company owns several apps and wants one
account to sign in to all of them. The hub is its own project, deployed on a
domain of its own. Apps sign in through it with
`@jskit-ai/auth-provider-oidc-core` (pattern `auth/oidc-sign-in`).

## Do not use when

Do not use it inside an app that has its own users only: use local accounts.
Do not add it to an existing app as a second purpose; the hub's cookies and
pages belong on their own origin.

## Product decisions

- The hub's address (`APP_PUBLIC_URL`), on a domain no app shares.
- The owner (`OIDC_HUB_OWNER_EMAIL`): only this verified account opens Apps,
  People and Setup.
- The email sender (`OIDC_HUB_EMAIL_FROM` with `RESEND_API_KEY` or `SMTP_URL`).
- Optional "Continue with Google" with the owner's own Google OAuth client
  (`OIDC_HUB_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`, `OIDC_HUB_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET`), redirect URI
  `{APP_PUBLIC_URL}/hub/google/callback`.
- Development addresses approved automatically
  (`OIDC_HUB_DEV_ORIGIN_PATTERNS`, comma-separated `https://` globs where `*`
  stays inside one DNS label). Loopback is always included.

## Invariants

- Secrets (`OIDC_HUB_SECRET`, `OIDC_HUB_REGISTRATION_TOKEN`, sender keys,
  Google secret) live in the host's secret store, never in source.
- Every production app address waits for one owner click in Apps. Names are
  self-asserted; the full address is what the owner approves.
- Apps receive the authorization code flow with PKCE only, no refresh tokens,
  exact redirect URIs, and the same `sub` everywhere.
- The issuer and `/hub` paths are never framed; in production no hub page is.
  (Development lets an editor's preview pane show the hub's own pages.) The
  hub's own sign-in is first-party: apps never see passwords.
- Passwords use the JSKIT local-account scrypt v1 format, so local accounts
  import unchanged.

## Framework APIs

Install `@jskit-ai/oidc-issuer-core` with a database driver
(`@jskit-ai/database-runtime-mysql`). Its provider mounts on the app's Fastify
server:

- `/.well-known/openid-configuration` and `/oidc/*`: the issuer, built on
  `oidc-provider` with a persistent Knex adapter;
- `/oidc/reg`: protected self-registration (RFC 7591/7592) with the
  registration token as the initial access token;
- `/hub/interaction/:uid`, `/hub/google/*`, `/hub/api/*`: the hub's sign-in,
  account and admin API that the app's own pages call.

Add `HUB_GLOBAL_PATHS` from `@jskit-ai/oidc-issuer-core/server` to the
server's global UI paths so a surface-filtered server still serves them.
Pages send `x-hub-request: 1` on every state-changing call.

Commands (`jskit-oidc-issuer`): `keys rotate`, `import-accounts --in <file>
[--apply]` (dry run by default), `preview-identity`.

## Example files

`example/package.json` declares the hub runtime. `example/.env.example` names
every variable without values. `example/server/hubPaths.js` shows the one
server change.

## Variation points

Page design, wording and branding are the app's. Development origin patterns,
the email sender and Google are configuration. The registration policy,
security headers and token rules are not variation points.

## Verification

- Start with a missing variable and read the one-sentence error.
- Register a loopback app: it is approved automatically and signs in.
- Register an https app on another domain: it waits until Approve.
- Rotate the signing key: old ID tokens verify for two hours, then fail.
- Import exported local accounts with a dry run first; an imported account
  signs in with its old password.

## Avoid

- running the hub on a domain an app shares
- approving an app by its name without reading its address
- copying secrets into source or into the hub's Env defaults
- turning on development interactions or refresh tokens for apps
